content: The relationship between physical activity and cancer risk is not fully understood. A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted following the MOOSE guidelines to evaluate whether physical activity during youth and throughout life reduces the risk of breast, colon, and endometrial cancers. Relevant observational studies published up to July 2018 were identified through searches in PubMed and Web of Science. Studies included prospective cohort, case-cohort, nested case-control, historical cohort, and case-control designs that examined the association between physical activity and cancer risk. A random-effects meta-analysis was used to calculate the relative risk (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for the highest versus lowest levels of physical activity. Eighty publications were included in the analysis. For breast cancer, menopausal status did not significantly alter the inverse association observed. The findings suggest that engaging in physical activity from early childhood and maintaining it throughout life may reduce the risk of developing breast, colon, and endometrial cancers. A systematic review of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was conducted to assess the effects of resistance exercise on sleep quality and quantity. Impaired sleep is linked to increased morbidity and mortality, and exercise is considered a non-pharmacological intervention to improve sleep. Thirteen studies were included, showing that chronic resistance exercise improves all aspects of sleep, particularly sleep quality. However, combining resistance exercise with aerobic exercise attenuates these benefits compared to aerobic exercise alone. The acute effects of resistance exercise on sleep remain inconsistent and poorly studied. Resistance exercise also improves anxiety and depression, suggesting it may be an effective intervention for enhancing sleep quality. Further research is needed to explore the acute effects of resistance exercise on sleep, underlying physiological mechanisms, changes in sleep architecture, and its efficacy in clinical populations with sleep disturbances. A meta-analysis of cohort studies investigated the relationship between physical activity and lung cancer risk in men, women, and high-risk populations such as smokers. Twenty cohort studies involving nearly 3 million participants and over 31,000 lung cancer cases were included. An inverse association was found between physical activity and lung cancer risk, with stronger effects observed among smokers compared to non-smokers. These findings suggest that increased physical activity may lower lung cancer risk, particularly in smokers. Large interventional studies are needed to confirm these results. A meta-analysis evaluated the impact of programmed exercise lasting at least six weeks on anxiety symptoms in midlife and older women. The analysis included RCTs comparing exercise interventions to no intervention. Exercise was classified as mid-term (12 weeks to 4 months) or long-term (6 to 14 months) and ranged from low-intensity activities like walking and yoga to moderate-intensity aerobic and cardiovascular training. The results showed that mid-term exercise interventions of low-to-moderate intensity significantly improved mild-to-moderate anxiety symptoms in this population. A systematic review and meta-analysis examined the effects of physical exercise on cognitive function in adults aged 50 and older. Physical exercise, including aerobic, resistance, multicomponent training, and tai chi, was associated with significant improvements in cognitive function. Exercise sessions lasting 45–60 minutes at moderate intensity were particularly beneficial. These findings support recommending both aerobic and resistance exercise to improve cognitive function in older adults, regardless of their baseline cognitive status. A systematic review analyzed the effects of chronic and acute physical activity on working memory performance in healthy individuals. Chronic physical activity showed a small but significant improvement in working memory, while acute physical activity had no significant effect. Factors such as age and exercise intensity influenced the outcomes. The review highlighted the need for large-scale, high-quality RCTs to better understand the relationship between physical activity and working memory performance. A systematic review of workplace-based health promotion programs examined their impact on employee sleep duration. Twenty studies met the inclusion criteria, with interventions utilizing various behavior change techniques. The findings suggest that workplace health promotion programs may improve sleep duration and subsequent daytime performance. A meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies explored the relationship between physical activity and incident depression. The analysis included 49 studies and found that higher levels of physical activity were associated with a reduced risk of developing depression.
